# Tell If a Job Application Was Written by AI Using Hugging Face's Free Detector

> **In short:** Paste a candidate's cover letter into Hugging Face's free AI-text detector and you'll get a percentage score suggesting how likely the writing is AI-generated. It's fast and free, but the score is a hint — not proof — so use it as one signal among several, not as the reason to reject an application.

When a stack of cover letters lands in your inbox, the polished ones can start to blur together. Sometimes a sentence reads too perfectly — every benefit tied to a skill, every paragraph ending on a confident note. You might wonder whether a real person sat down and wrote it, or whether the applicant clicked a button first. A free detector from Hugging Face can give you a quick read, and you don't need a tech background to try it.

## Before you start
- A modern web browser on any device — phone, tablet, or computer.
- A copy of the cover letter you want to check (a Word doc, PDF, or plain text is fine).
- About 5 minutes per letter, including reading the result.
- No account or payment needed for the basic detector page.
- An honest mindset: this tool guesses. It does not give you a courtroom verdict.

## Step 1 — Open the Hugging Face AI detector in your browser

In your browser's address bar, type `huggingface.co` and press Enter. Once the page loads, look for a search box near the top — it's usually labeled something like **Search models, datasets, users…**. Click inside it and type **AI text detector** (or **OpenAI detector**), then press Enter. From the list of results, pick the option whose description mentions detecting AI-generated text; the page that opens is usually called a **Space** (Hugging Face's name for a small interactive demo).

If you can't find it by searching, try going directly to the Spaces section and browse the **Text Generation** or **Natural Language Processing** category — the detector is usually near the top of that list. The page will look like a chat-style box on the left and a short explanation on the right.

**You'll know it worked when** you see a text box with a button beneath it — something like **Submit**, **Compute**, or **Run**. Don't click anything yet.

## Step 2 — Copy the cover letter text

Open the cover letter you want to check. If it's a PDF, select all the text (Ctrl+A on Windows, Cmd+A on Mac) and copy it (Ctrl+C / Cmd+C). If it's an email, click into the message, select all, and copy. You want plain text — not a screenshot, not a scanned image, because the detector only reads typed words.

Back on the Hugging Face detector page, click inside the empty text box on the left and paste your copied text (Ctrl+V / Cmd+V). The pasted letter should fill most of the box.

💬 Example: a short, generic cover letter paragraph — *"I am writing to express my strong interest in the marketing coordinator position at your company. With three years of experience in social media management and a proven track record of increasing engagement, I am confident I would be a valuable addition to your team."*

**You'll know it worked when** you see the candidate's words sitting inside the box, with no strange symbols or missing letters. If the paste looks broken, recopy from a plain-text source.

## Step 3 — Run the check

Look beneath the text box for the action button. It usually says **Compute**, **Submit**, or **Run**. Click it once. Then wait. The detector is doing math on the words you pasted, which usually takes a few seconds but can stretch to a minute when the site is busy.

Don't refresh the page, don't paste more text, and don't click the button again — that just queues another check and slows things down further. If the page feels frozen for more than two minutes, refresh and try once more.

**You'll know it worked when** a result appears on the right side of the page, or directly below the button, usually as a percentage or a colored bar.

## Step 4 — Read the result carefully

The detector typically returns two numbers side by side. One is labeled something like **Real** or **Human**, and the other says **Fake** or **AI**. Together they add up to 100%. A result of "98% Fake" means the detector thinks AI almost certainly wrote the text. A result of "62% Real" means it leans toward human — but not by much.

What you're looking for is the gap. A clear reading (above about 90% on either side) is more meaningful than a borderline one (say, 55/45). Borderline results are the detector saying, in effect, "I'm not sure," and you should treat that as "no useful signal" rather than a verdict either way.

**You'll know it worked when** you can point to one of the two percentages and say out loud which way the detector leaned, and by how much.

## Step 5 — Cross-check with your own judgment

Now read the cover letter yourself, like a person, not a detector. Look for things the detector can't see: does the letter mention a specific project from your company? Does it reference something only a real applicant would have noticed on your website? Are there small, human imperfections — an awkward phrase, a typo, a personal detail about why this job?

A candidate who clearly read your job posting and wrote something specific to you is almost certainly a real person, even if the detector says otherwise. A candidate whose letter is generic, full of "I am a highly motivated professional"-style filler, and also scores high for AI on the detector is a stronger double signal.

**You'll know it worked when** you can combine the detector score with the actual content of the letter and arrive at a clearer sense of what you're looking at.

## Step 6 — Decide what to do next (and don't make it the only reason)

Treat the detector as one piece of evidence in a pile that includes the resume, the interview, the references, and your gut. Hiring decisions based on a single AI-detection score can push out strong candidates who happen to write in a flat, polished style, and they can also let through applicants who lightly edited an AI draft.

If the score is clear and the rest of the application raises real questions, that's worth a follow-up conversation. If the score is borderline or the rest of the application is strong, move forward normally.

**You'll know it worked when** you can explain, to yourself and to the candidate if asked, why you made the call you made — and the detector is just one sentence in that explanation.

## Common mistakes
- **Trusting a borderline score as a verdict.** Anything between roughly 40% and 60% on either side is the detector hedging, not deciding. Treat it as no signal at all and look at the letter with your own eyes.
- **Pasting a screenshot or scanned image.** The detector reads typed text only. If you paste an image, you'll either get an error or a meaningless score. Always copy plain text.
- **Letting the score override good evidence.** A candidate who names a specific product you sell, references a recent news item about your company, or describes a hands-on project in detail is very likely a real person. Don't reject them because the detector disagreed.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** If you volunteer to read applications for a school board, a community group, or a local club, this tool gives you a fast first-pass filter when something feels off — without needing to pay for software.
- **For your business or work:** In a hiring funnel with hundreds of applicants, the detector can flag letters that are worth a closer look. Pair it with a short writing prompt of your own ("tell us, in your own words, why you want this job") so applicants get a fair chance to show their real voice.
- **If you're just getting started:** Run the detector on a cover letter you wrote yourself, then on a paragraph you ask an AI assistant to draft. Seeing the two scores side by side teaches you faster than any description can.

## Try it now
Open `huggingface.co`, search for **AI text detector**, paste a paragraph from the last cover letter you read, and click **Compute**. In under a minute, you'll see a number that either surprises you or confirms what you already suspected — and you'll know what to make of it next time.
